claims.text: Introducing short-range-order precipitates into a crystalline semiconductor reduces its lattice thermal conductivity relative to the pristine material.
Intrinsic silicon is an example of a high-quality crystalline semiconductor suitable for studying lattice heat conduction.
Heat in the proposed crystalline semiconductor is primarily conducted by lattice phonons.
SRO precipitates can be introduced controllably within a crystalline semiconductor matrix.
The relevant measurements should be performed in a temperature range where lattice heat conduction dominates.
The temperature range where lattice heat conduction dominates is typically below the onset of substantial electronic conduction and above the Debye temperature.
The density and spatial distribution of SRO precipitates constitute the structural mediator of the proposed effect.
SRO precipitates act as phonon-scattering centers.
Enhanced phonon scattering reduces phonon lifetimes.
Enhanced phonon scattering reduces phonon mean free paths.
Reduced phonon lifetimes and mean free paths decrease lattice thermal conductivity.
Samples containing engineered SRO precipitates will exhibit a statistically significant reduction in lattice thermal conductivity relative to pristine crystalline controls.
The proposed effect applies when phonons dominate heat conduction, such as in insulators or intrinsic semiconductors.
An optimized precipitate size and distribution can scatter mid-to-high-frequency phonons without introducing additional heat-conduction channels.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity reduction depends on precipitate density, size, spatial distribution, and temperature.
A pristine sample of the same crystalline semiconductor provides the experimental control.

The hypothesis is falsified if precipitate-containing samples show neither a statistically significant reduction in lattice thermal conductivity nor a measurable change in phonon-scattering characteristics relative to pristine samples.
